..

Through next Thursday...

Satellite imagery shows flat ridging over the northern Rockies
shifting slowly to the east, as a deep Pacific trof digs near the
BC coast. The upstream trof is our weather-maker for the weekend,
but in the meantime we have to deal with the ridge for one more
day.

Today will be very hot and dry per enhanced downslope winds/ 
warming in a pre-frontal regime. Temps will be in the 80s to near
90F and some daily records could be broken. Min RHs will fall to 
near or below 10% many areas, with the assistance of breezy SW
winds which will gust 35-45 mph along the western foothills. A Red
Flag Warning remains in effect for the western and southern
foothills (areas that did not see significant rainfall in
September and have much drier grasses). Tonight will be another
mild night w/ poor RH recovery. Still looks like some modest
downslope gusts could impact the lee side of the Beartooths and
Bighorns late tonight and this will need to be monitored. A cold
front arrives early Saturday bringing an end to the recent warm
and dry stretch of weather, finally.

Expect brisk north winds and falling temps on Saturday, along with
increasing chances of showers in the west as an upper low forms
over the PacNW. The low will continue to push southward Sunday & 
Monday, a bit west of what would be ideal for precip here, but the
combination of ascent, upslope flow and anomalously high 
atmospheric moisture will yield a good period of precipitation. 
All of this is of high confidence at this point. Mountains will 
see heavy snow (60-70% chance of 12+ inches above 8kft) and a 
Winter Storm Watch has already been issued for the Beartooth 
Absaroka & Crazy Mountains. The heavy snow will likely also 
include the Melville Foothills on the east side of the Crazies, 
per deep E-SE flow. The bigger questions concern surface temps, 
ptype and whether or not snow will be able to accumulate at lower 
elevations. 

Today's models have trended warmer in the boundary layer and thus
the potential for accumulating snow east of the foothills has
trended down. The air mass we will tap into is currently in 
AK/Yukon. There seems to be two pieces of colder air, the colder
of which is shown to stay in northern Canada while the lesser cold
sags thru AB into MT. This seems to give some credence to the
warmer model solutions, but must also stress continued high spread
among ensembles. The other uncertain piece of the puzzle is
moisture from Rachel, a hurricane still west of Baja. Pwats are
expected to rise to near 200% of normal in our cwa this weekend as
moisture is drawn northward in the highly amplified SW flow aloft.
Would expect a surge of heavier precip over our east Sunday Night
into Monday, but models differ here. One thing to be more
confident of is that surface temps look to stay sufficiently warm
to keep ptype as rain over the east, but cannot rule out snowfall
over the higher hills. Generally speaking, the highest potential 
for snow accumulation at lower elevations is west of Billings. For
Billings itself, believe it will snow but struggle to accumulate,
with the possible exception of the higher hills surrounding the 
city. Small temperature changes would mean big differences in the
weather we see. The chance of 2+ inches of snow is near zero in 
the east, about 10% at Billings, and 50-80% along the western 
foothills. Impacts from any heavy snow would include travel, 
outdoor recreation, and weighing down of tree limbs and possible 
tree damage. Look for temps in the 30s & 40s Sunday & Monday.
Please continue to monitor the forecast as additional adjustments
will be necessary.

Before moving on we should address actual precipitation, which
will be widespread and significant. Ensembles show totals of 
0.25-0.50" in the east and 1-1.5" in the west. Western mountains
could see more than this, as could the east, depending on the
exact track and impacts of Rachel's moisture.

The upper low will eventually cut off over the SW CONUS and the
passage of a weak zonal wave will end our precip sometime Monday
or Monday evening. After a dry & warmer Tuesday (temps in 50s to
near 60F) things get more interesting again. There is increasing 
confidence that the SW low will eject to the north and clip 
southeast MT with a good chance of showers (rain) Wednesday. At 
the same time, another Canadian wave arrives and possibly phases 
with the low, continuing the chance of precip through Thursday. By
Wednesday night and Thursday temps could cool enough for wet snow,
and the northerly flow would favor southern upslope areas (a 
different scenario than the initial weekend system). Expect temps 
near 60F Wednesday then upper 40s and 50s Thursday. JKL
